questions.question: A 14-year-old boy collapses during sport. He was taking erythromycin and there is a family history of sudden death. What is the cause of syncope?
questions.exp: Erythromycin (a macrolide) prolongs the QT; with a family history of sudden death this points to congenital long QT unmasked by the drug. HOCM also causes exertional syncope, but the drug clue favours LQTS.

questions.question: What is a possible cause of myocardial infarction in children?
questions.exp: MI in children is rare: Kawasaki coronary aneurysms, anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA), familial hypercholesterolaemia and Williams syndrome.

questions.question: A baby born at 32 weeks by caesarean section weighs 1.2 kg; the mother is obese. Which of the following is NOT associated with later obesity in the child?
questions.exp: The recall keyed caesarean section. Note that observational studies link CS with a slightly higher obesity risk, while LBW with catch-up growth and maternal obesity are stronger risks.

questions.question: A child has features of Kawasaki disease. What is the management?
questions.exp: IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever onset plus aspirin; steroids are added for high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases.

questions.question: A 26-week preterm born because of pre-eclampsia becomes severely distressed on day 4 and is ventilated. Platelets are 50 ×10⁹/L and falling. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Early thrombocytopenia (first 72 h) from pre-eclampsia/placental insufficiency is mild and stable; new or falling platelets after 72 hours with deterioration suggests late-onset sepsis or NEC. The recall first marked placental insufficiency, then corrected to sepsis.

questions.question: What is the prevalence of anorexia nervosa in adolescent girls?
questions.exp: Anorexia affects about 0.3–1% of adolescent girls; bulimia is more common (1–3%).

questions.question: A neonate is cyanosed with a weak thready pulse. Which is NOT associated with cyanotic congenital heart disease?
questions.exp: Cyanosis comes from right-to-left shunting or mixing; a pure left-to-right shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA) is acyanotic.

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl playing with toys suddenly develops respiratory distress with bilateral crackles (more on the right), reduced air entry on the right and hepatomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilateral crackles with hepatomegaly suggest heart failure (e.g. myocarditis). A foreign body gives unilateral signs without hepatomegaly. The recall keyed heart failure.

questions.question: A 5-year-old has a limp after a URTI and is afebrile. What is the management?
questions.exp: Transient synovitis: rest and NSAIDs; review if fever or not improving in 48–72 hours.

questions.question: A child has a limp, will not move the leg, and has a temperature of 39 °C. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fever, refusal to bear weight and painful restricted joint movement = septic arthritis until proven otherwise (Kocher criteria).

questions.question: A boy has a painful, swollen, red knee for weeks with two fever episodes. Aspirate is turbid with mainly lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chronic monoarthritis with lymphocytic turbid fluid suggests TB (or Lyme); pyogenic arthritis is acute with neutrophils.

questions.question: A 14-year-old on growth hormone therapy develops a limp; X-ray confirms the diagnosis. What is the management?
questions.exp: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a recognised complication of GH therapy; treat with in-situ screw fixation, non-weight-bearing until surgery.
questions.d: Surgical pinning to prevent avascular necrosis

questions.question: A girl has axillary lymphadenopathy and mediastinal widening on chest X-ray. What is the best test for diagnosis?
questions.exp: Excision biopsy of an accessible node gives histology for suspected lymphoma.

questions.question: A boy has a sore throat and lymphadenopathy and develops a rash after amoxicillin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Amoxicillin rash in EBV infection is common and not a true allergy.

questions.question: A girl has low mood and abnormal movements of her arms 2 weeks after a URTI; ASO titre is high. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Post-streptococcal neuropsychiatric disorder: abrupt OCD, tics or chorea with emotional lability after GAS infection. Sydenham chorea is a major criterion of rheumatic fever (treat with penicillin prophylaxis).

questions.question: A child with Down syndrome has fatigue, irritability, cyanosis, features of pulmonary hypertension and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the plan?
questions.exp: Uncorrected VSD/AVSD with Eisenmenger physiology is no longer operable; discuss prognosis and palliative options with the family.
questions.a: Discuss possible management and prognosis with the parents

questions.question: Which is NOT a criterion for withholding or withdrawing treatment?
questions.exp: RCPCH framework: limited quantity of life (brain death, imminent death), limited quality (unbearable burden) or informed refusal by a competent patient — but a child's refusal alone does not usually decide life-sustaining treatment. The recall keyed the competent child option.
questions.b: Preterm with no signs of viability
questions.c: A competent child consents to withhold treatment

questions.question: A teenage girl has a facial and skin rash, arthritis and neurological signs, with high triglycerides, high ferritin and raised soluble CD25. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: SLE features (rash, arthritis, neurological) with HLH markers (ferritin, triglycerides, sCD25). The recall wrote 'SLE with primary HLH'; in SLE the HLH is secondary (autoimmune-associated).

questions.question: A study of drug side effects reports p = 0.01. What does this mean?
questions.exp: A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true; p<0.05 is conventionally significant.
questions.b: The probability that the result occurred by chance alone is less than 1 in 100
questions.c: The drug has side effects and must not be used

questions.question: A child in status epilepticus received lorazepam in the ambulance. Gas: pH 7.2, PCO2 8, HCO3 14, BE −18; glucose 2.1 mmol/L. What is next?
questions.exp: Correct hypoglycaemia immediately (2 mL/kg 10% dextrose); it may cause or prolong seizures.

questions.question: A neonate with hyperinsulinism has frequent hypoglycaemia and is given diazoxide. Which is NOT an effect of diazoxide?
questions.exp: Diazoxide opens beta-cell K-ATP channels to reduce insulin release; it is a vasodilator (lowers BP) and causes fluid retention and hypertrichosis.

questions.question: A child has abdominal and back pain with microscopic haematuria. What is the best test?
questions.exp: The recall keyed Ca:Cr ratio (hypercalciuria/stones). In practice ultrasound is also first-line for loin pain with haematuria.

questions.question: A girl with poorly controlled diabetes has fatigue, abdominal pain and sweet-smelling breath in clinic. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Ketotic breath with abdominal pain suggests DKA: urgent ED assessment, fluids and insulin.
questions.d: Stop insulin and change to oral agents

questions.question: A 14-year-old obese girl (weight 90th centile) has truncal obesity, abdominal striae, acanthosis nigricans and irregular periods. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Purple striae with truncal obesity suggest Cushing; check height velocity (falls in Cushing) and late-night salivary cortisol. PCOS is commoner and the recall was unsure.

questions.question: A pregnant woman asks about the triple test for Down syndrome. What does it include?
questions.exp: Triple test: AFP, hCG, unconjugated oestriol; adding inhibin A gives the quadruple test.

questions.question: A tall boy (height 90th centile) whose father is also tall has shortness of breath and chest pain and is followed by cardiology. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant tall stature with cardiac follow-up (aortic root dilatation) = Marfan; chest pain may be aortic dissection or pneumothorax.

questions.question: A child recently arrived from India has a musty odour and fair hair. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Untreated PKU: musty odour, fair skin and hair, eczema, learning disability and seizures.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT included in the UK newborn screening programme?
questions.exp: UK blood spot screens 9 conditions: sickle cell, CF, congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1 and homocystinuria. Galactosaemia is not screened. (The recall's options were all screened conditions; this item was rebuilt.)

questions.question: A neonate collapses with HR 240 and receives adenosine. Echo shows multiple intracardiac masses. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Multiple cardiac rhabdomyomas are the earliest sign of tuberous sclerosis; they may cause arrhythmia (WPW) and usually regress.

questions.question: An 8-year-old is lethargic, tired and not concentrating at school; he is obese and short. Which test is LEAST useful?
questions.exp: Obese and short suggests an endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, Cushing) and sleep apnoea explains poor concentration. A metabolic screen is low yield. The recall was uncertain.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered basic (laboratory) research?
questions.exp: Basic research works on mechanisms (cells, animals); RCTs are clinical research.
questions.a: Studying cell mechanisms of a drug in leukaemic cells
questions.d: A randomised controlled trial comparing two groups

questions.question: An 8-year-old has fever and sore throat; the rapid strep test is negative. While awaiting culture, which antibiotic is most appropriate if one is started?
questions.exp: If antibiotics are indicated for GAS pharyngitis, penicillin V for 10 days is first-line; macrolides only for penicillin allergy.

questions.question: A child with eczema has crusted, bleeding (punched-out) papules. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Punched-out erosions and crusted vesicles in eczema = eczema herpeticum: urgent IV/oral aciclovir. The recall marked bacterial infection; impetiginised eczema gives golden crusts.

questions.question: A child has a gluteal abscess growing Pseudomonas, recurrent serous otitis media, lymphadenitis and failure to thrive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Deep abscesses and lymphadenitis with failure to thrive suggest a phagocyte defect (CGD).

questions.question: When investigating immunodeficiency, which test is matched INCORRECTLY?
questions.exp: DHR (dihydrorhodamine) flow test is for CGD; SCID is assessed with lymphocyte subsets and T-cell function.

questions.question: Which is the LEAST likely complication of gestational diabetes in the baby?
questions.exp: Fetal hyperinsulinism causes macrosomia, hypoglycaemia, RDS, polycythaemia and hypocalcaemia. IUGR occurs in pre-existing diabetes with vasculopathy, not GDM.

questions.question: A neonate born by breech delivery has reduced right arm movement; the arm is pronated and flexed at the wrist. Which roots are affected?
questions.exp: Erb palsy (C5–C6): adducted, internally rotated arm, extended elbow, pronated forearm, flexed wrist ('waiter's tip'). Klumpke (C8–T1) gives a claw hand.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl has early-morning vomiting for 2 months and now an unsteady gait. What is the best investigation?
questions.exp: Morning vomiting with ataxia suggests a posterior fossa tumour; MRI is the investigation of choice (CT if MRI not available urgently). The recall keyed CT, then wrote MRI.

questions.question: A teenage girl has weight loss, irritability, tremor and goitre with a high free T4. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Graves is the commonest cause of hyperthyroidism in adolescents (TSH receptor antibodies). Hashimoto may cause transient hyperthyroidism but usually hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A teenage girl with anorexia nervosa took a paracetamol overdose. What is the plan?
questions.exp: In any overdose check paracetamol and salicylate levels and consider co-ingestants; low body weight increases toxicity risk.
questions.b: Paracetamol level and screening for other drugs, which cannot be excluded

questions.question: What is the first-choice antibiotic for early-onset neonatal sepsis?
questions.exp: NICE: benzylpenicillin with gentamicin covers GBS, E. coli and Listeria (amoxicillin if Listeria suspected).

questions.question: A 19-day-old has poor feeding, fever and skin vesicles. What do you give?
questions.exp: Vesicles in a febrile neonate suggest HSV: start IV aciclovir with antibiotics and investigate (HSV PCR of lesion, blood, CSF).
questions.a: Antibiotics for 14 days and aciclovir until results

questions.question: Which is NOT an indication to start antiepileptic medication after a first seizure?
questions.exp: NICE: consider treatment after a first seizure with neurological deficit, unequivocal epileptic EEG, structural abnormality or unacceptable risk. An equivocal EEG is not an indication.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has anaphylaxis. What is the first drug?
questions.exp: Under 6 years: 150 micrograms = 0.15 mL of 1:1000 IM. 1:10 000 is for IV use in cardiac arrest.

questions.question: A 2-month-old has horizontal nystagmus, especially on distance gaze, and keeps a head turn. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Infantile (congenital motor) nystagmus is horizontal, starts at 2–3 months and patients adopt a head turn to the null point. The recall was uncertain.

questions.question: Antenatal scan showed unilateral pelviureteric junction dilatation of 11 mm; postnatally it is bilateral. Which investigation is NOT urgent?
questions.exp: Bilateral dilatation needs early ultrasound, MCUG (exclude PUV/VUR) and urine testing; DMSA/MAG3 functional imaging is done later (6–8 weeks).

questions.question: A boy has bilateral hydronephrosis and a thick-walled bladder. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: PUV causes bladder outlet obstruction in boys: thick trabeculated bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, keyhole sign.

questions.question: A girl has features of hypothyroidism. Which is NOT an indication for routine thyroid screening?
questions.exp: Regular thyroid screening is advised in Down and Turner syndromes, type 1 diabetes and coeliac disease (autoimmune clustering).

questions.question: A 3-week-old has pale loose stools, poor weight gain and raised direct bilirubin. What is the working diagnosis?
questions.exp: Conjugated jaundice with pale stools needs urgent exclusion of biliary atresia (Kasai best before 45–60 days).

questions.question: A 2-week-old breastfed baby gaining weight well is jaundiced. What do you do?
questions.exp: Prolonged jaundice screen: split bilirubin first; most will be breast milk jaundice.

questions.question: Which is a contraindication to BCG vaccination?
questions.exp: BCG is a live vaccine: contraindicated in HIV, SCID and other immunodeficiency, and in infants exposed to biologics in utero.

questions.question: About contraindications to breastfeeding, which statement is NOT true?
questions.exp: Babies with PKU can have some breast milk with phenylalanine-free formula and level monitoring. Galactosaemia is an absolute contraindication.
questions.a: Hepatitis C is not a contraindication
questions.b: Neonates with phenylketonuria should not breastfeed
questions.c: Neonates with galactosaemia should not breastfeed
questions.d: Mothers with HIV in developed countries should not breastfeed

questions.question: What feature distinguishes Patau syndrome from Edwards syndrome?
questions.exp: Patau (trisomy 13): midline defects (cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly), polydactyly, scalp defects. Overlapping fingers are typical of Edwards; both may have rocker-bottom feet.

questions.question: A 12-year-old has recurrent infections, candidiasis, a heart murmur and past neonatal tetany. Which is NOT a feature of this condition?
questions.exp: 22q11 deletion: conotruncal defects, palatal anomalies, hypocalcaemia, thymic hypoplasia and learning difficulty. Renal anomalies occur in some, but renal agenesis is the recall's key.

questions.question: A 2-year-old with Edwards syndrome has respiratory distress and features of intestinal obstruction. What do you say to the parents?
questions.exp: Children with trisomy 18 who survive infancy may benefit from palliative surgery for comfort; decisions are shared with parents in their best interest.
questions.b: You will not intervene because of poor prognosis
questions.d: You will discuss surgery that relieves distress, as part of a shared plan

questions.question: A collapsed baby has cyanosis, poor thready pulses and a forceful apex. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Duct closure in HLHS causes shock with poor pulses and a dominant RV impulse; start prostaglandin.

questions.question: A mother had shingles 7 days before delivery and TB in the second month of pregnancy (treated). The baby has poor feeding and hypoactivity. What do you do?
questions.exp: Maternal shingles does not put the baby at significant risk (maternal IgG protects); treated TB earlier in pregnancy is low risk. A sick neonate needs a full sepsis work-up.
questions.b: Blood tests and investigations to find and treat the possible cause

questions.question: Which condition is inherited as autosomal dominant?
questions.exp: EB simplex is mostly AD. Albinism, CF and junctional EB are AR; incontinentia pigmenti is X-linked dominant. (The recall's answer was junctional EB, which is recessive.)

questions.question: A 5-year-old with sickle cell disease has severe pallor and abdominal pain after a viral illness with rash. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Parvovirus B19 (slapped cheek rash) stops erythropoiesis, causing aplastic crisis with low reticulocytes. Sequestration would give an enlarging spleen.

questions.question: A mother has SLE. What is a recognised risk for her baby?
questions.exp: Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies cause neonatal lupus: heart block, rash, cytopenias and hepatitis.

questions.question: A teenage girl has a rash on her knees and elbows and nail pitting. What else may you find?
questions.exp: Psoriasis with nail pitting: psoriatic arthritis may present with dactylitis ('sausage digits').

questions.question: A boy injures his hand while running; middle and ring fingers are mildly swollen with a small abrasion. What is true?
questions.exp: Minor soft tissue injury: analgesia, elevation and safety-net advice.
questions.b: Simple analgesia, and return if swelling increases

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl has 3–4 café-au-lait spots, each 0.4 cm. What is true?
questions.exp: NF1 needs ≥6 café-au-lait spots (>5 mm prepubertal) or other criteria; freckling appears later (3–5 years), so its absence does not exclude NF1. Review over time.
questions.b: Absence of axillary freckling makes NF1 unlikely
questions.d: She needs follow-up and investigation if the spots persist or increase

questions.question: Which lesion is present from birth?
questions.exp: Port-wine stains are capillary malformations present at birth and grow with the child. Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks and proliferate.

questions.question: A neonate with ambiguous genitalia has a female (46,XX) karyotype and normal electrolytes on day 1. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Virilised 46,XX: CAH is most likely; measure 17-OHP after 36 hours and urine steroid profile, monitor electrolytes (salt wasting appears at 1–2 weeks). Pelvic ultrasound shows the uterus.

questions.question: A child with abnormal behaviour has iron deficiency anaemia and pica (eating old paint). The blood film shows basophilic stippling. What do you do?
questions.exp: Lead poisoning: remove the source, treat iron deficiency, and chelate (DMSA, EDTA) depending on blood lead level.
questions.a: Explain the likely diagnosis (lead poisoning) and risks, give iron and start chelation
questions.d: Iron and refer to the community paediatrician

questions.question: Which of the following is LEAST likely to need investigation for thyroid disease?
questions.exp: Growth failure, falling school performance and goitre prompt thyroid tests; isolated behaviour problems usually do not.

questions.question: Which test compares means of a normally distributed continuous variable between two groups?
questions.exp: Parametric (normal) data: t-test; categorical data: chi-squared; non-parametric: Mann–Whitney.

questions.question: A child has polyuria, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with low potassium, and glycosuria. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Generalised proximal tubule failure: glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria and type 2 RTA. Bartter gives alkalosis.

questions.question: In a child with shock, which statement is NOT true?
questions.exp: Antibiotics are given when sepsis is suspected, not for every type of shock (e.g. hypovolaemic, anaphylactic, cardiogenic).
questions.b: Antibiotics are given to all children with shock
questions.c: Assessment, IV fluids and inotropes as required
questions.d: Oxygen is given regardless of SpO2 initially
